claims.statement: Mrs. Taylor took her case to attorney Frank A. C. MacManus, an old friend of her father, to gain access to him.
It was said that Allen made a will at the Baptist hospital the week before, leaving his championship cup and other property to Mrs. Tillie Hartgrove.
Allen's will is dated March 4, 193 (the year is cut off; the hint says March 24, 1903); its witnesses were Dr. Heine Marks, Dr. E. R. Newcomb and Charles Brock.
Simon S. Bass, named executor in Allen's will, refused to serve.
Public Administrator Garrard Strode took charge of Allen's estate, which was in a muddled condition.
Tillie Hartgrove, Allen's housekeeper, had a writ of replevin issued at Clayton for a driving horse held by William W. Heapes.
Gillespie got a policeman to help him take the saloon, but the policeman refused to interfere, and Gillespie decided not to risk his life.
Gillespie asked the officer to arrest Murphy, but the officer advised that a warrant be issued instead.
Friends of Tom Allen planned to apply to the probate court on Monday, April 6, 1903, for a conservator for him.
Polly Taylor was cut off with $10 in her father's will and says she will contest the will in the courts.
Gillespie said he had a claim against Allen for goods sold to him.
Allen's will was filed in probate court on Monday, April 6, 1903; it left $10 each to his two sisters and the balance to Mrs. Tillie Hartgrove.
Attorney Simon Bass filed Allen's will in probate court; it gave no estimate of the value of the estate and no inventory of his personal property.
Allen's daughter, Mrs. Mary Taylor, said she would apply to the courts to protect the property, which she alleged was being dissipated by people with no right to it.
Mrs. Mary Taylor said she would apply to the courts that day to secure protection for her father's property.
Constable Fred Lenz failed on April 21, 1903 to replevin the driving horse claimed by Tillie Hartgrove, Tom Allen's former housekeeper.
Judge Taylor denied Tillie Hartgrove a divorce from her husband, Martin Hartgrove, after learning she had been Tom Allen's housekeeper.
Tom Allen's estate has dwindled almost to nothing and is still in litigation.
Circuit Judge Taylor refused to grant Tillie Hartgrove a divorce from her husband, Martin Hartgrove.
Hartgrove and Gillespie left Clayton threatening to replevin (sue to recover) the hat.
Allen's widow, who lives in England, intends to contest the will and claim a dower interest.
The widow engaged St. Louis attorney F. H. Sullivan to bring the suit against the will.
The widow of Tom Allen demanded a dower interest in his estate, which is valued at $279.80.
Public Administrator Garrard Strode filed the inventory of Allen's estate in probate court on Tuesday, July 28, 1903.
The inventory valued Allen's estate, including his saloon, at $279.80.
Public Administrator Strode's appraisal, filed for record on 1903-07-28, valued Allen's estate at $279.80.
Public Administrator Garrard Strode filed an inventory of Tom Allen's estate in probate court.
